projects.title: Redondo Red — Stories to tell
projects.anecdote: The concept was Redondo on the run, fleeing south, dodging death at every corner. Then I found out Brendon and Tanya were about to have a baby, and the quieter story took over. We shot in their house, with their Cortez, their truck, their dog. A time capsule of their life, on celluloid. Full story inside.
story: When I first listened to Stories to tell, I knew the music video had to be an epic. And just like the content of the song, the process of making it became a self-reflective practice—unlocking meaning, identity, and importance along the way.

The initial concept had Redondo on the run—fleeing south across the border, dodging death at every corner. But with more playthroughs, and learning what was happening in Brendon’s real life, I realized there was a quieter, and far more monumental, story to tell.
Brendon and Tanya were expecting a child. Well—more than expecting. Tanya was basically about to pop.

But did that also mean Redondo Red was expecting a child?
Is the artist the man, and vice versa?
How do real-life moments—especially ones of pure, undeniable greatness—impact the identity of the artist?
Those questions danced around in my head as my DoP, Pedro, and I set out to film.

I’m still amazed by the honesty and involvement Brendon and Tanya brought to this. As I tried to navigate the heady tension between the Artist, the Man, and his Family, they offered every element of their real lives. Where we filmed is where they lived. The Cortez was theirs. The truck. The wardrobe. The dog… Hazel!
A time capsule of their life, caught on celluloid.
I’d rather not prescribe much more intention to the piece. It should speak for itself.

But do I think you’ll like it? Yes.
Is it true to heart? Absolutely.
Did I say what I meant to say? I’m not sure.
But hey—if I tried, and if I failed… at least I…

projects.title: Charli XCX — Used to Know Me
projects.anecdote: Nine costume looks in one day on 35mm. A brand partner leaves the video in post b/c cheerleader outfits and adult beverages do not mix (turned out to be an easy save). Found gold in a tricky edit. We caught lightning in a bottle to complete this video, her last Crash single before a bratty storm. Full story inside.
story: Like the lyrics to my favorite Widowspeak song, “everything is simple, ’til it’s not.” Used To Know Me sounds simple. One house, one day, Charli playing dress-up in a domestic fantasy that keeps escalating: bedroom, bathroom, Victorian, zesty nun, cheerleader, 1920s flapper pool, EDM rave, jazzercise, kitchen counter BDSM. Nine costume looks: the wigs, the makeup, the choreography for each of them. Shot on 35mm, three perf, on a Panavision package big enough that we had to raise our company’s insurance coverage just to rent it. Wait, simple?

The house was a mid-century place in Long Beach, on the same street as the house from Ferris Bueller’s Day Off, owned by people who worked in production themselves and knew exactly what they had. It was also the first house the creative team sent me, and after weeks of scouting alternatives the answer came back the way it always does when the creatives are right: this is the location. So my job became making the place affordable.

Halfway through prep, our DP told me the day only worked if we could light in a leap-frog manner, and that meant people and gear we hadn’t budgeted. He was right, btw. I went back for more money before the shoot and… I love Charli’s team :)

Then there were the brand integrations, which had to land (fast) with the choreography and song, or the day was gonna fall apart: an Amazon box in the cold open, packed so it would unwrap on camera in one move, and a perfectly misted drink glass by the pool for a one-shot the camera glides through. Both worked on the day. Charli had been drilling the choreography for weeks (we filmed just before her album tour) and a lot of the schedule quietly hinged on her nailing it. She nailed it.

One partner later watched the cut, decided a cheerleader outfit from a different moment signaled something their fizzy drink couldn’t align with, and left the video in post. The pool scene stayed. We removed the logo from the glasses of, you’ll never guess, Fanta? Yup! All’s well that ends well. Unless…

The first cut came back… flat: Charli in normal land, Charli contemplative on the toilet, then suddenly Victorian, with nothing in the cut carrying you from the real world into the imaginary one. Not to mention, the Amazon moment was taking too long at the top. We had to find a way. The budget for starting over was gone, and I was already doing some VFX on the intro, so I gave the recut to the only person left in the budget, me.

The 35mm was tack sharp (a first AC doing their job is a beautiful thing, and so is detail-preserving upscale in After Effects), which meant I could punch in and build camera moves we never shot. The first costume snap needed to feel like a jump between worlds. Star Fox spoke to me in a dream. I rolled the frame. It worked! The graphics team had made a different title card for every look, each one thematically gorgeous, so I splashed them in. My favorite adjustment came from addressing the Amazon Prime timing moment. The cut needed a runway at the top, so I needed sound. Taking a tactic from a 2-figure video, I accessed the UTKM stems, retimed, reverbed, and built a build to preamble the actual needle drop on this 6-figure video. I did not know if that was okay. When the creative director saw it, she really liked the intention, and had Charli’s music director make a custom track to fill that timing. I’m still so stoked on that.

The video came out, did good numbers, and everyone got paid real money (music videos sometimes only pay in stardust and dreams); the only casualty of the whole job was one ceiling light tile, which wasn’t actually broken, it had to be turned 90°. Used To Know Me was 4 years ago. If I got this job today I’d lock the brand architecture faster and put myself deeper inside the creative conversation from the start, which is not a note on anybody so much as what four more years of life and learning buys you.

Used To Know Me is positioned at a frontier point for Charli. Crash was the self-aware sellout album, and Used To Know Me was the last album single release before brat. My read, which is just my own, is that the energy was already all there, one album before it clarified. I’m not the lore person. But we love YouTube comments. Lightning went into a bottle. Then it came out.

projects.title: RÜFÜS DU SOL — Music is Better
projects.anecdote: Sand dunes night shoot, infinite-zoom oner, the VFX was the edit. Barely made it out alive. Fitzcarraldo, but the mountain was After Effects.
story: The video was supposed to work like this. You are inside a photograph. Then you are inside the next one, and the next, and it never cuts. An infinite zoom, dreamy and flash-lit and saturated, pulling you through image after image with the band inside every frame.

Before I was on this job, the team had commissioned a photographer whose AI work does exactly that, and does it beautifully. The plan was for her to make the video. She proved it couldn’t be done before anyone shot a frame. The models available in early 2024 could not hold the likenesses of three specific guys through the transformation, at that velocity, lip synced. The reference survived. The method didn’t. What was left was a beautiful idea, a delivery date, and nobody who had made something quite like this before.
So we shopped it. Every VFX house came back with the same shape of answer: yes, here are three ways, and all three cost more than the entire production budget.

The director found the Oceano dunes and wanted to go look, so we went. Him, the band’s management, my co-producer and me, in a Bronco. The public way onto that sand is to drive down onto the beach, off-road along it, and cross a tidal canal that’s only open at low tide. We made the crossing, got out and scouted. The place was gorgeous and completely unusable.

Two days later I found an RV campground whose back gate opens straight onto prime dune. No canal, no basecamp on open beach. The dunes ran west of the gate, so the sun set straight into our backgrounds at the end of the day. Real dunes were back on the menu.

The shoot was two days, both splits, afternoon into night. Day one was the dunes. The first setups were natural light with minimal grip, where “minimal” meant an 8x8 frame, sandbags, and a video village for client, hauled roughly 600 yards through loose sand. We shot the furthest-out setups first and retreated toward the campground as the sun dropped.

Day two was motels rented by the hour, from owners who were kind about a request that perplexed them. That night we invented a blackout scene in a parking lot, then ran around town with the band and one strobe, stealing stills.

In post it was hard to see an edit, because on this video the edit was the effect. Every setup was a locked-off plate that had to be rigged onto a moving scale rig and rendered before anyone could see whether a cut worked. We had about 40 seconds assembled when our editor had to jump to a prior obligation. He had helped invent the system and taught us how to wrangle it, bless him, and then he was gone, so I took over the cut.
Warning: very technical section.

The wall turned out to be a units problem. After Effects expresses scale as a percentage, and apparent velocity is not linear in percentage, so a pass-by that reads as continuous cannot be one object getting bigger. It has to be a relay race of nulls, each one scaling up and handing off to the next before it outruns usable resolution, with pre-comps strung onto them, each pre-comp carrying a performance that has to stay lip synced the whole way it travels. Then roto on all of it. Then the seams, because the plates were a mix of video and enormous stills, and at that scale the joins show.

So I ran content-aware fill in After Effects, took the frame into Photoshop, generated the missing material there, kept only the transparent region the fill had added, and tracked that patch back onto the moving plate. It works. I accept my Razzie for Most Deranged Method, thank you. The patch also drops track in the middle of a move, and pulls off register when parts of the frame parallax at different rates from center, which required even more noodling.

For the bridge, I stopped cutting and started building. I pulled the real dunes out of the plates, rebuilt the dune architecture in Blender, and ran a camera-speed-matched setup for a more graphical desert passage.
Pass-bys read continuous, the three faces stay themselves the whole way through.

If I got this job today, the first thing I’d do is insist on a VFX supervisor. I want to be precise about why I didn’t, because it wasn’t laziness or ego. Early on in prep, I knew enough to brainstorm the effect out loud. We could try it this way, or this way, what about this, and those ideas got yeses, and the yeses built trust, and the trust came back to me as “let’s go with your guidance on this.”
Knowledge you happen to have is not the same as knowledge you should be underwriting by yourself.

The second thing is structural. On this project the creative director was also the director and also, functionally, our executive producer, which means the same person hearing every creative ambition was hearing every logistics constraint, and was understandably very committed to landing the ambition. My co-producer and I were both freelance. There was nobody to bring a pure production concern to, because the person you’d bring it to was the person the concern was about.

That’s a diagnosis and not a complaint, and I know the difference because the same team’s next two videos had an actual executive producer from the management side, and simpler concepts, and both came out beautifully. Same band, same director’s eye, different structure, and nobody had to invent anything. That’s not a note on anybody. It’s what a missing chair at the table costs.
I rewatched it for the first time in a long time. When we finished I was too far inside it to see anything, and I think I assumed I’d never like it.
I actually think it’s a pretty cool video.

projects.title: AMIRI — Pacific Flat
projects.anecdote: One shot, 15 seconds, one model who keeps multiplying across a very detailed couch. Frankenstein compositing!
story: This was a VFX job where I felt like a fireman or something. My friend Jeff Prosser, a really talented director who’d been working in-house for AMIRI, brought me on for a 15-second spot for the Pacific Flat sneaker: one shot, one room, one model, except she keeps multiplying. The camera punches in on a shoe product detail, pulls back out, revealing another clone of her in the room. Repeat a few times. The way this effect is most easily done is with motion control: the camera repeats the exact same move every take, and the clone versions can stack more cleanly. We did not have motion control. They did do a great job with choreo, spacing, lighting consistency, and human camera operating. But it was still a crack-them-knuckles, grind-those-fingers post job!

The set was a beautiful sunken 1970s couch arrangement. My gorgeous nemesis. Zooming in on a foot stepping onto the ground would have been its own kind of challenge. Stepping onto a couch means the ground deforms. The cushion sinks, the seams bend, and every version of her had to press into the same fabric seeming at the same time. Those seams were a gift and a problem in equal measure: a grid I could line everything up against, and a grid the viewer could line everything up against too. Nothing could be smudged over while it was in frame. It became puppet tools and compositing stacked on compositing in After Effects, solve one problem, inherit a new one, layer on layer. If you saw under the hood… “bruh.”

The other half of the job was the timing. I retimed her walks take by take, then match-moved my digital zooms to the real camera operating, so the shot could hand off from a real push to a built one and back without you feeling the seam. There is one step where I had to splice her leg so her shin and foot are footfalling from one take and her other leg and upper body are from two other shots. I really hope you don’t know which one that was. This being a high-fashion ad, the product fidelity was not negotiable. Every one of those layers had to hold up at the resolution where you are admiring a shoe, and feeling the brand’s emotional benefits.

The final output is 15 seconds and looks effortless (unless you’re also a VFX artist). It’s right here and it’s short, just watch it. I’m glad Jeff called. The job inspired me: when I later creative-directed a campaign for a small fashion label called Field Journal, the first setup I wrote was a duplication moment. Check it out here.
projects.credits: dir Jeff Prosser · client AMIRI · JJ House: VFX

projects.title: Field Journal
projects.anecdote: Met a fashion designer at a birthday party; 7 days later, three friends and I shot a campaign for his label.
story: I met Jeffrey Siu at my friend Josh’s birthday party. Josh is a designer, his wife Isobel is a fashion designer, and Jeffrey, their friend visiting from Milan, consults on design for C.P. Company while bootstrapping a label of his own on the side: Field Journal. Jeffrey’s showing me photos on his phone. I see Field Journal creates backpacks, jackets, and oversized workwear jeans. All with awesome silhouettes. I’d done VFX on a Stone Island spot, so it was easy to talk techwear. My bold roommate was a great hype man and said, “Well, you two should make something.” Jeffrey, in town for ten more days, was down.

This is the most complete creative-direction job I’ve done. I spent a few days on a vision board and scripts, a set of fashion scenarios written loose enough to DIY on a hybrid stills-and-video day blasting around the South Bay. I got to make something real for a real brand, and Jeffrey got media for a label he was funding himself.

The thread I was pulling on: Jeffrey’s work is grounded, enriched-craftsman techwear, urban without being sci-fi. I kept thinking about what it means to be an honest person in a surveillance state. I was swirling the comic series Transmetropolitan and fun, kinetic cinema. So the setups played with that energy: existing inside watched, urban spaces, and subverting them.

The hero setup, which I called Spycraft, we shot at an indie storage facility in Redondo Beach, so liminal and cool. Its lobby had a comically big and obvious security camera, twenty-foot floor-to-ceiling mirrors with nothing extruding from them but alarm systems, an elevator up to a storage floor with a view of the semi-operational power plant (if you know the area, you’ll geotag it). I cut it in a thriller-narrow aspect ratio, over the Ocean’s Eleven soundtrack “$160 Million Chinese Man.” Luke Orlando, a director friend with a cinematography background and a great eye for this tone of work, shot it; he kept finding Dutch angles that stretched the frames and evoked the comic/manga that we both love. My actor friend Danny Cron modeled, bringing the whole mood alive.

I was inspired to do the duplication setup from the AMIRI job (that story is on this site too), scored with something uncanny and a little whimsical. Jeffrey ended up using the two hero videos. The thing that never ran anywhere official is my favorite: I took sequences of Danny into Photoshop and turned them into comic-strip pages. Nobody asked for them. I found them noodling in post. I love them. They’re below.
